https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: An estimated 200 activists gathered in Portsmouth and clashed with riot police on Sunday night. Photograph: Supplied View image in fullscreen An estimated 200 activists gathered in Portsmouth and clashed with riot police on Sunday night. Photograph: Supplied Portsmouth Police used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrest Minister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’ Rajeev Syal , Steven Morris and Ben Quinn Mon 7 Sep 2026 15.12 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”. No 10 condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right activists after Portsmouth unrest Read more After police contained the weekend’s second disruptive demonstration against asylum seekers travelling to the UK in small boats, it was claimed that officers in Hampshire were pushed off their motorbikes and pelted with bricks. Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, condemned groups behind the disorder for promoting “racism and thuggery”. Activists wearing balaclavas clashed with police in Portsmouth on Sunday evening after a dinghy reached the UK from Normandy. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary have launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage. Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked to Tommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, claimed to have arranged the protest. Thomas was also behind disruption in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port for several hours. View image in fullscreen Daniel Thomas, left, speaking to the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf (right, in blue suit), has claimed to have arranged the demonstration. Photograph: Theo Shaw/PA In a statement to MPs, Jones said: “Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary, with the support of other neighbouring forces, used a dispersal notice to ensure public safety and officers were forced to use batons and Pava spray to maintain order in the face of some aggression.” Spencer Wragg, the chair of the Hampshire police federation, said one of the officers injured was a rookie who had only finished training school three days earlier. “Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations,” he said. About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire after travelling to the UK on a “mega-dinghy” which had departed from the Normandy coast and was at sea for roughly 10 hours. The landing point of the dinghy was farther west than most small boat arrivals. Officials are concerned that people smugglers are starting to target new routes across England’s south coast, with craft launched from a wider stretch of the French shoreline. View image in fullscreen About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire at the weekend. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters An estimated 200 protesters gathered and clashed with riot police on Sunday night, vowing to prevent migrants leaving the port. Footage showed some chanting “send them back” as police officers with shields raised tried to maintain order. Amid concerns that police were caught unawares by the unrest in Dover on Saturday, Jones said: “Work is ongoing to establish any lessons and ensure that relevant intelligence is shared at pace across our law enforcement system.” Speaking to MPs and peers at a closed-door meeting on Monday, the prime minister Andy Burnham said Labour’s mission must be to counter “fear with positivity and hope”. Burnham is understood to have told the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) that Britain would never accept any form of racism in its communities and stood for a sense of fairness and justice. “We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” the prime minister said. “There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets. “We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.” Labour and Lib Dem MPs called on the government to explain why police appeared to have been caught off-guard by the events in Dover and Portsmouth. Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and a former Home Office minister, questioned why the police were not aware of plans to block the local port. “Please ensure that the intelligence picture is strong enough so that the police can respond accordingly to future incidents,” he told MPs. The Liberal Democrat Home Office spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, asked: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence? And how is it that then an apparently separate group with some commonalities were then able to blockade another site the next evening?” View image in fullscreen Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, said the government would learn lessons from the disorder. Photograph: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA Jones said there was “a crossover in terms of online activity” and the government would learn lessons from the disorder. In an on-camera confrontation on Monday, Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, told the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, that the Patriot Platform group he led would deliver working-class votes to Reform – but expressed anger at Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Dover demonstrators for wearing balaclavas. Thomas said: “I understand Nigel is going to be prime minister one day and I understand he has to set a standard, which will basically be that you know he can’t just come out and say, everything’s great and these guys are fantastic, but Nigel needs to be very careful with his words.” Yusuf said he would “take that message back” and added that Thomas had articulated why he and his group had organised demonstrations. “I think it’s important we listen to people. He was making his points respectfully,” he said. 10:30 Who is behind ‘thuggish’ far-right protests in Dover and Portsmouth? - The Latest Police could impose a balaclava ban on future anti-migrant demonstrations after officers were injured, Whitehall sources said. Under the Crime and Policing Act, Hampshire police could apply for a ban to ensure that protesters cannot cover their faces. Facebook posts claim that a demonstration is planned for Saturday by a group called Portsmouth Patriots. Hampshire police has been approached for comment. Ministers have been criticised for failing to condemn far-right groups behind the disorder. Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see. “We’ve got different ways to register our protest. We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.” The Hampshire and Isle of Wight police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said England’s south coast was not prepared for the arrival of migrants, and ministers would have a “significant issue” if people traffickers shifted their routes farther west. She warned that places such as Portsmouth were “not set up” for the arrival of migrants. Kent police defended the force’s action after it described the highly organised protest action in Dover as “spontaneous”. Assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the term was used in line with national guidance and that the action had “developed rapidly”. Eight boats carrying 625 people arrived in the UK on Sunday after crossing the English Channel, Home Office data shows. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/pak.text: The Budapest Times Paks crisis cost less and finished early – Magyar takes a swipe at Orbán’s record Work to raise the water level of the Danube in order to keep the Paks nuclear power plant operational has, in the summer of 2026, been "progressing faster and will cost less than planned for the first time in several decades," the Prime Minister declared at Thursday's session of the National Assembly, before the agenda. Péter Magyar also spoke about a new era of Hungary's water management and energy adaptation. The head of government explained that there had been several days this summer when Hungary simultaneously faced multiple crises and challenges that a state should have been preparing for over the course of decades. He listed an unprecedented drought, a heat dome, record heat, severe water shortages, record-low water levels on the Danube, and an energy crisis of historic proportions. He recalled that while the extreme heat meant electricity demand was higher than ever before, the country’s most important power plant was losing ever more of its generating capacity due to the extraordinary heat and the receding Danube. There was a moment, he added, when the Paks nuclear power plant was producing just 230 megawatts instead of its nominal 2,000 megawatts. Péter Magyar said there are moments in the life of a country when it becomes clear how the state is structured, how much its institutions are worth, how much the preparedness and work of its professionals count, how much a government’s capacity for decision-making is worth, and it also becomes clear “how much we can count on one another.” He pointed out that when Hungarian people and companies were asked to voluntarily reduce and reschedule their electricity consumption during the critical hours, they did so. He touched on the fact that, during this time, a struggle was underway at Paks “for every centimetre of the Danube’s water level,” with specialists measuring the river around the clock and the government holding an away session in Paks. He stated that the government did what a government’s job is in a crisis situation: once specialists say what is needed, the government decides and secures the resources, money, tools, personnel, and legal conditions required for implementation — and then lets those whose task it is get on with the work. He stressed that the work carried out to raise the Danube’s water level in the interest of operating the Paks power plant in the summer of 2026 “has, for the first time in several decades, progressed faster and will cost less” than planned. Péter Magyar, commenting on the work, emphasised: “it did not fall behind schedule, it did not end up costing three times as much, as everything does under the Orbán governments — instead it became faster and cheaper.” He stressed that the successful management of the crisis was not the success of the prime minister, a minister, the government, or the Tisza Party, but the shared success of Hungary and every Hungarian — the engineers, the soldiers, the water management professionals, the energy specialists, the companies, the workers, the families, the people. What the government had to contribute to their achievement was to make immediate decisions when needed and to ensure the funding and resources, he pointed out. He summed it up by saying that “this summer there were two Hungaries”: one worked, the other talked; one Hungary sought solutions, the other sought scapegoats; one Hungary was on the Danube, the other was holidaying at the seaside. One Hungary asked what still needed to be done to protect their homeland; the other asked how political capital could be made from it, said Péter Magyar, noting that a politician’s responsibility does not end when they go into opposition — and especially does not end after 16 years in government. He stated that there is nothing wrong with taking a holiday in itself — everyone needs rest, opposition politicians and the former prime minister included. The question is what they do when their country is facing a crisis unlike anything seen before, he said. He continued: Viktor Orbán led the country for 16 years, for nearly six thousand days. The state of the water management system, the problems with the cooling water system and pumps at Paks, and the vulnerability of the energy system did not develop over a hundred days — nor were the missed investments missed over a hundred days. He objected that when the consequences of these problems hit the country all at once, they received scaremongering and fake news from those who had governed for 16 years. The Prime Minister said he is not interested in what kind of boat Viktor Orbán is vacationing on or what beer he drinks — what interests him is where the leaders of the parliamentary parties were and what they did when the Hungarian people needed them. After 16 years, perhaps it is precisely the former prime minister and the former governing parties who should help reveal what investments were delayed and what professional warnings were received, he said. Péter Magyar added that in the autumn they will submit the new climate law and new water management regulations to the National Assembly, review the condition and protection of critical infrastructure as well as the reserve systems, and expand them if necessary. They will also review the investments that should have been launched years ago, and investigate why they were not. The Prime Minister said the entire country is grateful to those who took part in the works at Paks. At that moment, members of the Tisza faction in the chamber rose to their feet and applauded. According to Péter Magyar, what the country can take away from this crisis is the knowledge that it was capable of resolving it, as well as the lesson that such a situation must never catch it unprepared again. He stressed that the economy is increasingly dependent on a stable energy supply, and a responsible state must be ready for this. “We solved it together, jointly,” he said, adding that when trouble arose, the country could count on its people — the country remained functional, people did not turn against one another, they worked, helped, adapted, and found solutions. Péter Magyar closed his address by saying that Hungary had stood its ground, and that when trouble came again, it would stand its ground then too, because they are building a functioning, responsible, strong, and humane country that prepares itself for hardships. https://collider.com/most-badass-opening.text: By Marcel Ardivan Published Oct 3, 2026, 7:06 AM EDT Marcel is a writer who is passionate about most movies and series. He will watch anything that's good. He is a content manager by day and a videographer when needed. Marcel used to work at a major streaming service based in Asia Pacific as a Content Specialist and was the Distribution Manager for a local movie distribution company. Sign in to your Collider account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google Discover Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread 2 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap A great opening sequence can make a movie unforgettable before the story has even properly begun. Some films take their time introducing characters and establishing their worlds, while others immediately throw audiences into the action. These openings do more than grab attention: they establish the tone, introduce important characters, and often give us our first look at exactly what makes the movie special. From shocking gory kills to explosive action sequences, these are the opening sequences that know exactly how to make an entrance, leaving an immediate impression while also hyping up the audience for what comes next. The long-running James Bond franchise is famous for its great opening sequences, while notable directors like Christopher Nolan , Zack Snyder , and Quentin Tarantino have made a name for themselves for their memorable openings. So, here are the most badass opening sequences in movie history . 'Ghost Ship' (2002) Emily Browning as Katie Harwood screaming and crying in Ghost Ship Image via Warner Bros. Ghost Ship opens aboard the Italian ocean liner Antonia Graza in the 1960s. Wealthy passengers are enjoying a glamorous and carefree evening, and a little girl named Katie ( Emily Browning ) is seen dancing with the ship's captain as the band plays. Then, a mysterious figure pulls a lever attached to a thin metal cable. As the mechanism begins moving, the cable snaps across the deck, slicing through the passengers one by one . Bodies collapse across the dance floor, leaving only Katie alive. The deaths are shocking and brutal, as audiences do not expect this at all, especially because of how fast it all happened. Bodies are horrifically sliced, and we can see they're still struggling to piece their limbs back together. It's one of the most bone-chilling openings in a horror film. Unfortunately, nothing interesting happens afterwards , and the film is further marred by frenetic, incomprehensible editing that undermines the horror. '28 Weeks Later' (2007) Robert Carlyle running away and looking scared with other figures behind him in 28 Weeks Later. Image via 20th Century Studios The opening of 28 Weeks Later sees Don ( Robert Carlyle ) and his wife sheltering with a small group of survivors. Their small peace is broken when they decide to take in a survivor running from infected people. The zombies storm inside and start attacking them. In his helplessness and cowardice, Don abandons his wife, who desperately calls for his help, and runs away from the horde to the river, where he escapes with a boat. It's a hard task to follow up the generational 28 Days Later , yet this opening sequence for the sequel hits all the right notes. It introduces the audience to an unconventional character who is a coward but still relatable . The scene where Don is running in the field chased by hungry zombies as the iconic "In a House - In a Heartbeat" track plays is very cool. Despite being scared, Don still fends off some zombies, including his acquaintance who turned into an infected, from getting to his boat. The central conflict where he abandons his wife plays a big part in the film later on, which makes this opening highly memorable and effective. 'GoldenEye' (1995) Pierce Brosnan, as James Bond in GoldenEye, prepares to bungee jump Image via MGM/United Artists GoldenEye opens with James Bond ( Pierce Brosnan ) infiltrating a Soviet chemical-weapons facility, jumping from the top of the dam and parachuting down towards the facility. There he meets up with another agent, 006 ( Sean Bean ). The mission quickly becomes a race against time when Bond needs to destroy the facility. His partner is captured, leaving Bond no choice but to demolish the facility with bombs. The Bond franchise is famous for its exciting cold opens , and Brosnan's films have memorable openings ranging from action-packed to ridiculous. In his first outing as Bond, the opening sequence is elegant and impactful . The bungee jump, which was filmed at the Contra Dam in Switzerland, set a record for the highest bungee jump off a fixed structure. GoldenEye primed audiences for a new version of Bond from the get-go . The film has no shortage of action sequences, including the famous tank chase scene, explaining why it's often dubbed by fans as the best film in Brosnan's era. 'Tenet' (2020) Image via Warner Bros. The opening of Tenet takes place in Kyiv, Ukraine, as a group of shadowy men is attacking a packed opera house. Among them is the Protagonist ( John David Washington ), who seems to be an agent working on two sides. He tries to retrieve an unknown package, while the group tries to bomb the place to cover their tracks. During this operation, he witnesses something weird: a shootout is happening backwards in time. After a mysterious man helps him, he keeps the collateral damage to a minimum, but his cover is blown. Christopher Nolan has a reputation for incredible opening sequences. Tenet is arguably his most ambitious film yet, and this opening shows that he's pulling all the stops, turning a Soviet-era concert hall in Estonia into a playground for his spy film. The action-packed sequence teases the inversion element that is crucial in the film. Moreover, it shows the resilient and resourceful nature of this nameless protagonist . Do you think everything moves too fast in this sequence? As the film says, don't think too much about it; feel it instead. C OLLIDER Collider · Quiz Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Personality Quiz Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like? Paul Atreides · Captain Kirk · Princess Leia · Ellen Ripley · Max Rockatansky Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one. 🏜️ Paul Atreides 🖖 Capt. Kirk ✊ Princess Leia 🔦 Ellen Ripley 🔥 Max Rockatansky FIND YOUR HERO → QUESTION 1 / 8 LEADERSHIP 01 How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher? The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you. A I absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward. B I read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes. C I rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction. D I assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission. E I don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 2 / 8 STRENGTH 02 What is your greatest strength in a crisis? The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails. A Prescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly. B Improvisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one. C Conviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire. D Composure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury. E Endurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 3 / 8 MOTIVATION 03 What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for? Your deepest motivation is your truest compass. A The survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it. B The safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind. C Freedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire. D The truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not. E The one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 4 / 8 PEOPLE 04 How do you relate to the people around you? Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are. A With intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated. B With warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself. C With directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it. D With professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family. E With wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 5 / 8 THREAT 05 You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do? How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything. A Prepare in silence. If they won't listen, I'll be ready when they finally have to. B Keep pushing until someone listens — and if no one does, handle it myself. C Build the case, find the allies, and make the threat impossible to ignore. D Document everything. The truth matters even if no one believes it yet. E Stop trying to convince anyone. Survive it. That's the only argument that counts. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 6 / 8 COST 06 What has your heroism cost you personally? Every hero pays. The question is what — and whether they'd pay it again. A My innocence — I've seen what I'm capable of, and I can't unsee it. B People I loved — the command chair has a view, but it's a lonely one. C A normal life — I gave up everything ordinary the moment I chose the cause. D My sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise. E Almost everything — and I'm still not sure what I'm carrying it all for. But I keep going. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 7 / 8 RULES 07 How do you feel about the rules of the world you're in? Every hero has a relationship with the system. What's yours? A I understand them deeply — and I know exactly which ones must be broken, and why. B I respect the spirit of them and bend the letter when the situation demands it. C The system is the problem. I'm not here to work within it — I'm here to dismantle it. D I follow protocol until protocol stops being useful. Then I make the call myself. E The rules collapsed a long time ago. What's left is instinct, and mine are reliable. NEXT QUESTION → QUESTION 8 / 8 PURPOSE 08 When everything is on the line, what keeps you going? The answer is the most honest thing about you. A Destiny — or something that feels so much like it that the difference no longer matters. B The people on my ship — their faces, their trust, the fact that they're counting on me. C The belief that what we're fighting for is worth every sacrifice, including this one. D Sheer refusal to let it win — whatever it is. I don't stop. That's just who I am. E I'm not sure anymore. But the road is still there, and I'm still on it. REVEAL MY HERO → Your Hero Has Been Identified Your Sci-Fi Hero Is… Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible. Arrakis · Dune Paul Atreides You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become. You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you. You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape. Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway. That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you. USS Enterprise · Star Trek Captain Kirk You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet. You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously. Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it. Kirk's genius isn't tactical — it's human. He reads people, bends rules with purpose, and wills outcomes into existence through sheer conviction. That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours. The Rebellion · Star Wars Princess Leia You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of. You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable. You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back. Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion. That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you. The Nostromo · Alien Ellen Ripley You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters. You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself. Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan. You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there. When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything. The Wasteland · Mad Max Max Rockatansky You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril. You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply. Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words. Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting. That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours. ↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ 'Drive' (2011) Drive - 2011 - The Driver (Ryan Gosling) looks in his rearview mirror Image via FilmDistrict Drive opens by following the Driver ( Ryan Gosling ) as he takes on a getaway job for two criminals. After picking up his car from Shannon ( Bryan Cranston ), he moves into position. Meticulously looking at the time and listening to police radio, he waits for the criminals to get out. Then, the Driver has to evade the police and blend with the crowd, succeeding. This opening effortlessly establishes the Driver as extraordinarily capable . Ryan Gosling barely needs to say anything (he does not say a lot in this movie anyway), and audiences can see his confidence and meticulousness from the way he drives and how he sees his surroundings. Nicolas Winding Refn avoids making the sequence feel like a conventional action-movie car chase by shooting from the car's point of view , putting the audience practically in the Driver's seat. The whole sequence is accompanied by a minimalistic yet highly intense score by Cliff Martinez , which heightens the atmosphere. 'Watchmen' (2009) The Comedian (Jeffrey Dean Morgan) being thrown out a window in 'Watchmen.' Image via Warner Bros. Pictures Just like the graphic novel, Watchmen begins with the murder of the Comedian ( Jeffrey Dean Morgan ) inside his luxurious apartment. Blake, who is just enjoying himself watching television, is attacked by a masked man who is as skilled as he is. Blake throws the attacker across the room and onto the floor, but his opponent ultimately gain
